verdict.reasoning: Patient opens with: "I keep having a headache."

Location and timing: Patient says, "It's on the left side at the back" and "Yesterday, about mid morning." This is consistent with an acute new-onset left-occipital headache starting yesterday mid-morning.
Severity: Doctor asks 0–10 scale and patient replies, "Say about 8."
Character: Patient describes it as "quite intense and kind of quite throbbing."
Onset: Patient says, "It kind of built up gradually over a short period of time."
Associated symptoms: Doctor asks about "nausea, vomiting" and patient answers "No, nothing."
Photophobia: Doctor asks, "Any funny lights or anything like that in your vision area? Any problems when you look into the light?" and patient answers "No."
Vision changes: Doctor asks about "blurred vision" and "funny lights" and patient replies "No" to both.
Fever: Doctor asks, "Any high fever? Are you feeling shivery, sweaty?" and patient replies, "No, no fever."
Neck stiffness is not asked about by the doctor nor mentioned by the patient in the transcript, so a reported absence of neck stiffness is new information.
Rash: Doctor asks, "Any rashes at all?" and patient replies "No."
Sleep: Doctor asks, "And last night, did you manage to sleep through the night?" Patient replies, "Yes, I did."
Focal neurological symptoms: Doctor asks about "tingling, numbness, weakness anywhere?" and patient replies, "No, nothing," indicating no focal neurological symptoms.
Past medical history: Doctor asks, "And have you got any other medical problems?" and patient replies, "No, I haven't."
Chronic medications: Doctor asks, "Anything you take medication for?" and patient replies, "No, I don't."
OTC ibuprofen and effect: Patient says, "I took some Nurofen yesterday." Doctor asks, "did that make any difference?" Patient replies, "Not really."
Medication: Patient clearly states, "I took some Nurofen yesterday."
Doctor asks, "Any over the counter medications or allergies?" Patient replies, "No, only the Nurofen I took yesterday, Ibuprofen," implying no allergies reported.
Family history: Patient states, "My mother's had hypertension..."
Family history: Same sentence, patient adds, "and she does get migraines."
Living situation: When asked, "Who do you live with at home?" patient replies, "My partner."
Occupation: Doctor asks, "what's your job day to day?" Patient replies, "I'm a designer."
Smoking: Doctor asks, "And do you smoke at all normally?" Patient replies, "No, I don't."
Alcohol: Doctor asks, "Do you drink any alcohol regularly?" Patient replies, "No."
Drugs: Doctor asks, "And any other drugs?" Patient replies, "No."
ROS neuro: Doctor asks about "tingling, numbness, weakness anywhere?" and patient replies, "No, nothing," indicating a negative review for focal neurological symptoms.
Assessment restates: new-onset, unilateral left-back-of-head ("It's on the left side at the back"), intensity 8/10 ("Say about 8"), onset yesterday ("It started yesterday" / mid-morning).

History confirms absence of fever, vomiting, and rash, and no focal neuro deficits, but neck stiffness is not asked about or reported in the transcript; claiming its absence as part of no red flags adds information.
Doctor states, "trying slightly stronger pain relief. So similar to ibuprofen, but taking it instead of ibuprofen, not at the same time, and taking that regularly with food."
Doctor adds, "You can take paracetamol along with that."
Supportive care: Doctor advises, "Try and take rest, have lots of good hydration."
Safety net: Doctor advises contacting if "the pain's getting worse or you get new symptoms, feel fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, or you keep getting episodes of the same type of thing."

Doctor plans a new NSAID: "trying slightly stronger pain relief. So similar to ibuprofen... taking that regularly with food" and later mentions medication "that I prescribed from the pharmacy," with instruction not to take it at the same time as ibuprofen.

Doctor says, "If it's getting worse or not settling in the next day or two, then certainly give us a call back when you try the medication..." which corresponds to 24–48 hours or worsening/new symptoms.
Doctor refers to "the medication that I prescribed from the pharmacy," implying follow-up includes picking it up from the pharmacy.
